summary: This document describes a BGP mechanism that reduces the harm done to routing when BGP restarts. It defines an End-of-RIB marker, a Graceful Restart capability for announcing the ability to preserve forwarding state, and procedures to keep routing information across a TCP session reset. It updates RFC 4271 and was later updated by RFC 8538.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router reboots, its neighbors can keep using their old maps for a short time instead of panicking. This lets traffic keep flowing while it comes back.

questions: what happens to bgp routes when a router restarts
subtitle: How BGP routers keep forwarding traffic while a neighbor restarts, instead of tearing routes down.

tldr.problem: When BGP restarts on a router, its peers see the session go down and up. This routing flap causes route re-computation, update churn and possible transient blackholes and loops.
tldr.mechanism: A Graceful Restart capability announces that a speaker can preserve forwarding state. Peers keep the restarting router's routes marked as stale until it re-establishes the session, and an End-of-RIB marker says the initial update is complete.
tldr.outcome: Restarts cause less routing disruption, but transient loops or blackholes are still possible if routing changes before convergence. The RFC is updated by RFC 8538.

facts.label: Tuple layout
facts.value: AFI 16 bits, SAFI 8 bits, flags 8 bits

today: RFC 4724 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4271. It is updated by RFC 8538.

sections.title: The Problem of Routing Flaps
sections.content:
Normally when BGP restarts on a router, every peer sees the session go down and come back up. This routing flap triggers BGP route re-computation, routing updates and churn in forwarding tables, and it could spread across multiple routing domains. It can create transient forwarding blackholes or loops, and it uses control plane resources on affected routers.

RFC 4724 defines three pieces to limit this: an End-of-RIB marker, a Graceful Restart capability, and procedures for temporarily retaining routing information across a TCP session termination and re-establishment. It applies to all routers, including those that cannot preserve forwarding state, which need to implement only a subset.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, when one router blinks off, everyone nearby throws away their notes and starts over. That causes a lot of needless fuss.

sections.title: End-of-RIB Marker and Capability
sections.content:
The End-of-RIB marker is an UPDATE message with no reachable NLRI and empty withdrawn NLRI. It tells a peer that the initial routing update after session establishment is complete. For IPv4 unicast it is an UPDATE of minimum length. For other address families it is an UPDATE holding only an MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute with no withdrawn routes for that AFI and SAFI. Sending it is recommended for routing convergence in general.

The Graceful Restart Capability has capability code 64. Its value holds a 4-bit Restart Flags field, a 12-bit Restart Time in seconds, and 0 to 63 tuples of AFI (16 bits), SAFI (8 bits) and Flags for Address Family (8 bits).

  • The most significant Restart Flags bit is the Restart State (R) bit. When set, the speaker has restarted and its peer MUST NOT wait for its End-of-RIB marker before advertising routes to it.
  • Restart Time is the estimated time for the session to be re-established.
  • The Forwarding State (F) bit per address family, when set, says forwarding state for those routes was preserved during the restart.

Reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt. A capability with no AFI/SAFI tuples means the sender cannot preserve forwarding state but supports the Receiving Speaker procedures. A speaker MUST NOT include more than one instance, and a receiver ignores all but the last.
sections.plainLanguage: The marker is a note saying "that is everything I know for now." The capability is a name tag that says "I can restart politely, and here is how long I need."

sections.title: Restarting and Receiving Speakers
sections.content:
The router whose BGP restarted is the Restarting Speaker. Its peers are Receiving Speakers. A speaker MAY advertise the capability for an address family if it can preserve forwarding state, and is recommended to advertise it even if it cannot, to signal that it will send End-of-RIB and supports peers that restart. The End-of-RIB marker MUST be sent once the initial update for an address family is complete. A suggested default for Restart Time is a value less than or equal to the HOLDTIME in the OPEN.

The Restarting Speaker MUST retain forwarding state for BGP routes in its Loc-RIB, if possible, and mark it stale, without treating stale entries differently when forwarding. It MUST set the Restart State bit in its OPEN. It sets the Forwarding State bit only if forwarding state was indeed preserved, unless configuration allows otherwise. It MUST defer route selection for an address family until it receives End-of-RIB from all peers (excluding those with the R bit set and those without the capability) or the configurable Selection_Deferral_Timer expires. Then it updates forwarding state, removes stale information and advertises its Adj-RIB-Out.

When a Receiving Speaker detects the TCP session ending, it MUST retain the routes from that peer for the address families in the capability and mark them stale. If it did not notice the old session end, it MUST treat a new connection from the peer as ending the old one, close the old TCP session without sending a NOTIFICATION, and keep the new one. If the session is not re-established within the advertised Restart Time, it MUST delete the stale routes. Once re-established, stale routes for an address family are removed immediately if the F bit is not set, the family is missing, or the capability is absent. Otherwise, fresh updates replace stale routes, and on receiving End-of-RIB it MUST immediately remove routes still marked stale. A configurable upper bound on retaining stale routes MAY be supported.

Normal BGP procedures MUST still be followed when the TCP session ends because a NOTIFICATION message was sent or received.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbors keep the restarting router's old directions in a drawer, marked "maybe outdated." When fresh directions arrive, the old ones are swapped out. If the router never returns, the drawer is emptied.

sections.title: Changes to the BGP State Machine
sections.content:
The RFC edits the BGP finite state machine in RFC 4271, Section 8.2.2. In the Idle state, resource initialization now leaves out the resources needed to retain routes for graceful restart.

In the Established state, if a new TCP connection is established and the capability with one or more AFIs/SAFIs was received for the session, the system retains the routes, releases other resources, drops the old TCP connection, sets ConnectRetryCounter to zero, starts the ConnectRetryTimer and moves to Connect. If a TcpConnectionFails event arrives and the capability was received, the routes are retained and the state changes to Idle. A NOTIFICATION message still deletes all routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The router's rulebook gets a few new lines saying "if your friend said they might restart, do not throw their stuff away when they disappear."

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Graceful restart reduces routing flap effects, but not entirely. If a capable router restarts without preserving forwarding state, for example after a power failure, or if routing information changes before routers finish updates, transient routing loops or blackholes are possible. If not all IBGP speakers are Graceful Restart capable, exposure to these can increase.

The Restart Time, the bound on retaining routes and the bound on deferring route selection may need tuning as deployment experience grows. The benefit is also reduced in an Autonomous System where the IGP and BGP are tightly coupled, both restart, and the IGP has no similar Graceful Restart Capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Saving the seat helps, but if the room changes while your friend is away, someone can still get confused for a bit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because a new connection can end an old one, this might seem to open the door to denial of service. The RFC notes that unauthenticated BGP is already vulnerable to denial of service through attacks on TCP, and that TCP is commonly protected with the MD5 signature option, which equally protects against spurious new connections.

An attacker who opened a connection impersonating a peer could replace the real one and possibly advertise bogus routes. The window is small, because the legitimate peer would open a new connection and end the attacker's, so the attack devolves to denial of service. The RFC concludes it does not change the underlying BGP-4 security model.
sections.plainLanguage: A stranger could pretend to be your friend and take the saved seat, but the real friend would quickly come back and push them out.

fields.name: Restart Flags
fields.desc: Top bit is the Restart State bit; the rest are reserved.

fields.name: Restart Time
fields.desc: Estimated seconds to re-establish the session.

fields.name: AFI
fields.desc: Address Family Identifier; repeated per tuple.

fields.name: Flags for Address Family
fields.desc: Top bit is the Forwarding State bit; the rest are reserved.
